mmaths-2024-team-01.title: Each element covers 7 numbers
mmaths-2024-team-01.body:
An element $x\in S$ "equals" exactly the numbers $x-3,\dots,x+3$, which is $7$ consecutive integers. To cover $2024$ numbers we need at least $\left\lceil\frac{2024}{7}\right\rceil=290$ elements ($289\cdot7=2023<2024$). $290$ suffice: take $x=4,11,18,\dots$ (every $7$th number starting at $4$) so that blocks $[1,7],[8,14],\dots$ are covered; the $290$th block $[2024,2030]$ contains $2024$.

**Answer: 290**

mmaths-2024-team-02.title: Track last digits
mmaths-2024-team-02.body:
$a_1=0$, $a_2=0^1+1=1$, $a_3=1^2+1=2$, $a_4=2^3+1=9$, $a_5=9^4+1=6562$, so $a_5$ ends in $2$. From then on: $a_6\equiv2^5+1\equiv3$, $a_7\equiv3^6+1\equiv0$, $a_8\equiv0^7+1\equiv1$, $a_9\equiv1^8+1\equiv2$, $a_{10}\equiv2^9+1\equiv3$, $a_{11}\equiv3^{10}+1\equiv0$, $a_{12}\equiv0+1=1$. The last digits cycle $2,3,0,1$ with $a_n$ ending in $1$ exactly when $4\mid n$ (the exponent only matters mod $4$ for $2$ and $3$, and powers of $0$ and $1$ are trivial). Since $4\mid2024$, the last digit of $a_{2024}$ is $1$.

**Answer: 1**

mmaths-2024-team-03.title: Count by first digit
mmaths-2024-team-03.body:
For first digit $d$ ($1..9$), count pairs of digits $(e,f)$ with $e+f<d$: $\binom{d+1}{2}$ pairs $=\,1,3,6,10,15,21,28,36,45$. The total is $165$ out of $900$, so the probability is $\frac{165}{900}=\frac{11}{60}$ and $a+b=71$.

**Answer: 71**

mmaths-2024-team-04.title: Minimize by sharing
mmaths-2024-team-04.body:
To keep the area small, place the new triangles so that one triangle covers two open sides of squares at once. Move $1$ gives the triangle (area $\tfrac12$). In move $2$ two unit squares are attached to its legs, and one triangle fits into the corner between them, covering one open side of each square: area $\tfrac12+2+\tfrac12=3$. Continuing with the same economy, the shape becomes a diagonal strip growing by area $2$ per move, so after move $n\ge2$ the area is $2n-1$. For $n=2024$: $2\cdot2024-1=4047$.

**Answer: 4047**

mmaths-2024-team-05.title: Unfold the reflection at 0
mmaths-2024-team-05.body:
Reflect the board: a walk on $\{-5,\dots,5\}$ in which every step is $\pm1$ with equal probability, where we keep only the absolute value (the reflecting rule at $0$ is the same as taking $|x|$). After $5$ steps one player's position is $|2k-5|$ where $k\sim\text{Bin}(5,\tfrac12)$. So the distribution of the final space is: $5$ with probability $\frac{2}{32}$, $3$ with probability $\frac{10}{32}$, $1$ with probability $\frac{20}{32}$. The probability the two players coincide is
$$\left(\tfrac1{16}\right)^2+\left(\tfrac5{16}\right)^2+\left(\tfrac58\right)^2=\frac{1+25+100}{256}=\frac{126}{256}=\frac{63}{128}.$$
So $a+b=63+128=191$.

**Answer: 191**

mmaths-2024-team-06.title: Eliminate possibilities
mmaths-2024-team-06.body:
Claire's number is not prime and (since she answers "No" without knowing Cat's exact number) is not a multiple of any of $10,\dots,19$. The two-digit numbers like that are $21,25,27,35,46,49,58,62,63,69,74,81,82,86,87,92,93,94$. "Telling the digits would not reveal my number" means the reversed number also qualifies (with distinct digits): only $49$ and $94$ remain.

Cat knows Claire's number is $49$ or $94$ and states that his number is not coprime to hers; for him to be sure, his number must share a factor with both: among $10..19$ only $14$ works ($14=2\cdot7$, $49=7^2$, $94=2\cdot47$). Claire now knows Cat's number is $14$; she says they share the ones digit, so her number is $94$ (ones digit $4$), not $49$. Product $14\cdot94=1316$.

**Answer: 1316**

mmaths-2024-team-07.title: Sum over all 21 choices
mmaths-2024-team-07.body:
There are $\binom72=21$ ways to choose the two multiplication signs. Add the values of all $21$ expressions:

- Adjacent signs give products $n(n+1)(n+2)$ for $n=1..6$: $6+24+60+120+210+336=756$.
- Non-adjacent signs give two separate products $n(n+1)$. The product $1\cdot2$ and $7\cdot8$ each appear $5$ times and every other $n(n+1)$ appears $4$ times: $2\cdot5+(6+12+20+30+42)\cdot4+56\cdot5=730$.
- The terms left as additions: the numbers $1$ and $8$ stay added in $\binom62=15$ choices; the others in $\binom52=10$ choices: $15(1+8)+10(2+3+\dots+7)=135+270=405$.

Total $756+730+405=1891$, average $\frac{1891}{21}$ (coprime, as $1891=31\cdot61$). So $m+n=1912$. (Brute-force enumeration confirms $1891$.)

**Answer: 1912**

mmaths-2024-team-08.title: Reflect to a chord of the circle on diameter BC
mmaths-2024-team-08.body:
$B,C,E,F$ lie on the circle $\omega$ with diameter $BC$ (right angles at $E$ and $F$). Reflect $E$ over line $BC$ to $E'$, also on $\omega$. Since $AD$ is the altitude and bisects $\angle FDE$ (true in every acute triangle), the line $DF$ makes the same angle with $BC$ as $DE'$, so $F,D,E'$ are collinear. Hence $FD+DE=FD+DE'=FE'$, a chord of $\omega$, so it is at most the diameter $BC=6$.

Equality needs $FE'$ to be a diameter through $D$, i.e. $D$ the midpoint of $BC$; this happens for $AB=AC=7$, which is an acute triangle. So $m=6$ and $m^2=36$. (Numerically, over all valid $AB$ the maximum of $FD+DE$ is $6$.)

**Answer: 36**

mmaths-2024-team-09.title: Strategy analysis
mmaths-2024-team-09.body:
There are four $2\times2$ squares. Grant's best first move is the center, which belongs to all four. Call a $2\times2$ square blocked once Stephen occupies a cell in it.

If Stephen's reply is on an edge cell (probability $\frac12$ of his second move being an edge, i.e. $4$ of the $8$ cells), Grant plays the opposite edge. Then, with probability $\frac13$ Stephen's next move leaves two unblocked squares and Grant can get three X's in one unblocked square while another remains unblocked: he wins with probability $\frac34+\frac14\cdot\frac12=\frac78$; otherwise Grant is left with a single unblocked square and three X's, and wins unless Stephen blocks the last cell: $\frac34$. So the win probability is $\frac13\cdot\frac78+\frac23\cdot\frac34=\frac{19}{24}$.

If Stephen replies in a corner, Grant plays an opposite edge and a similar analysis gives $\frac23\cdot\frac78+\frac13\cdot\frac34=\frac{20}{24}$.

Overall $\frac12\cdot\frac{19}{24}+\frac12\cdot\frac{20}{24}=\frac{13}{16}$, so $m+n=13+16=29$. (An exhaustive expectimax computation over the game tree confirms $\frac{13}{16}$.)

**Answer: 29**

mmaths-2024-team-10.title: Congruent triangles and a rotation
mmaths-2024-team-10.body:
Since $\angle CBD=90^\circ+\angle ABC=\angle EBA$ (the angle at $B$ in both triangles is $90^\circ$ plus an angle of the triangle), and $\angle AEB=\angle DCB$ and $AE=DC$, triangles $AEB$ and $DCB$ are congruent. So $DB=AB=11$ and $EB=CB=10$, and triangle $AEB$ is a $90^\circ$ rotation of triangle $DCB$ about $B$; hence the lines $EA$ and $CD$ are perpendicular, and $\triangle APC$ has a right angle at $P$.

Now $\angle EBD$ and $\angle ABC$ are supplementary (the full angle around $B$ is $360^\circ=90^\circ+90^\circ+\angle ABC+\angle EBD$). The Law of Cosines in $\triangle EBD$: $400=100+121-220\cos\angle EBD$, and in $\triangle ABC$: $AC^2=100+121-220\cos\angle ABC=221+220\cos\angle EBD$. Adding, $AC^2+400=2\cdot221$, so $AC^2=42$. Then $CP^2=AC^2-AP^2=42-16=26$.

**Answer: 26**

mmaths-2024-team-11.title: Arrange the sequence in an $m\times m$ grid
mmaths-2024-team-11.body:
Write $a_{m,0},a_{m,1},\dots,a_{m,m^2-1}$ in rows of length $m$. The first row is all $1$'s ($a_{m,k}=1$ for $k<m$ since $a_{m,k-m}=0$), and the first column is all $1$'s (since $n\equiv0\pmod m$). Every other entry is the sum of the entry to its left and the entry above it ($n-1$ and $n-m$). This is Pascal's rule, so the entry in row $i$, column $j$ (0-indexed) is $\binom{i+j}{i}$. The last entry ($i=j=m-1$) is $a_{m,m^2-1}=\binom{2m-2}{m-1}$.

Therefore the ratio is $\dfrac{\binom{4048}{2024}}{\binom{4046}{2023}}=\dfrac{4048\cdot4047}{2024\cdot2024}=\dfrac{4047\cdot2}{2024}=\dfrac{4047}{1012}$ (using $\binom{2k}{k}=\frac{2k(2k-1)}{k^2}\binom{2k-2}{k-1}$). $4047=3\cdot19\cdot71$ and $1012=4\cdot11\cdot23$ are coprime, so $a+b=4047+1012=5059$.

**Answer: 5059**

mmaths-2024-team-12.title: Optimize the extreme sizes
mmaths-2024-team-12.body:
We may assume one set per size, with consecutive sizes $s,s+1,\dots,t$ (so $m=t-s+1$) and sums strictly decreasing as the size grows. The smallest-size set has sum at most the sum of the $s$ largest elements, $\frac{s(2N-s+1)}{2}$ with $N=10000$; the largest-size set has sum at least $\frac{t(t+1)}{2}$. The $m$ sums must be distinct integers, so we need
$$\frac{s(2N-s+1)}2-\frac{t(t+1)}2\ge m-1=t-s.$$
Conversely when this holds, every size class can realize any sum between its minimum and maximum possible sums, so the intermediate sets can be chosen. Scale by $N$: with $s=aN$ and $t=(a+\mu)N$ (so $m\approx\mu N$), the condition becomes $a(2-a)\ge(a+\mu)^2$ up to lower-order terms, i.e. $\mu\le\sqrt{a(2-a)}-a$. This is maximized when $2a^2-4a+1=0$, i.e. $a=1-\tfrac1{\sqrt2}$, giving $\mu=\sqrt2-1$. So $m\approx(\sqrt2-1)\cdot10000\approx4142$ (an exact integer search with the inequality above gives $4142$; the official solution estimates $4143$). Either way $\lfloor m/100\rfloor=41$.

**Answer: 41**
